# chapter: # Sources live in resources/sources/01/ (SOURCES.md). Complaint = United States v. Thompson, MJ19-0344, Doc. 1 (allegations). CA9 = 9th Cir. No. 22-30179 (2025-03-17). OCC = Consent Order #2020-036. Judgment 2025 = W.D. Wash. 2:19-cr-00159-RSL Doc. 462 (2025-10-29).

claim as made in prose: FBI arrested Thompson on 29 July 2019; search warrant executed that day; devices referencing Capital One seized
The GitHub gist timestamped 21 April 2019 contained a server IP address, code for three commands, and a list of more than 700 buckets
DOJ arrest release: "The intrusion occurred through a misconfigured web application firewall that enabled access to the data"
Wikipedia: Thompson "had previously worked as a software engineer for Amazon Web Services"; "about 140,000 Social Security numbers"; 106 million people
source: Wikipedia, "Capital One", § July 2019 data breach, fetched 2026-09-01 (wikipedia-capital-one.txt)

claim as made in prose: Krebs 2 Aug 2019, citing a source: misconfigured open-source WAF; SSRF attack relaying to the metadata service; role "allowed to list all of the files in any buckets of data, and to read the contents of each of those files"
The complaint was sworn by FBI SA Joel Martini on 27 July 2019 and filed 29 July; it names the provider only as "the Cloud Computing Company"

Complaint: "A firewall misconfiguration permitted commands to reach and be executed by that server, which enabled access to folders or buckets of data in Capital One's storage space at the Cloud Computing Company"
The words SSRF, metadata, Amazon and AWS do not appear in the complaint
source: Complaint, all 12 pp. (OCR'd text searched; complaint-ocr-raw.txt and complaint.txt)

claim as made in prose: On or about 12 March 2019 an IP address controlled by IPredator (Swedish VPN provider) attempted to access Capital One's data

On or about 22 March 2019 the *****-WAF-Role account executed List Buckets several times from believed Tor exit nodes and Sync a number of times, obtaining files containing credit card application data
According to Capital One, the *****-WAF-Role account does not, in the ordinary course of business, invoke the List Buckets Command
A List Buckets call ran on 21 April 2019 from an IPredator address; its timestamp matches the gist; the gist address included Thompson's full name

On 17 July 2019 at 1:25 AM a previously unknown individual e-mailed Capital One's responsible-disclosure address: "There appears to be some leaked s3 data of yours in someone's github / gist … Let me know if you want help tracking them down"

Capital One determined on 19 July 2019 that an intrusion had occurred; the vulnerability was reported via its Responsible Disclosure Program on 17 July; "We immediately fixed the issue and promptly began working with federal law enforcement"

Complaint ¶11: three commands — first obtained credentials for *****-WAF-Role; second (List Buckets) listed bucket names; third (Sync) copied data from buckets "for which the *****-WAF-Role account had the requisite permissions"
Capital One re-ran the commands and confirmed they functioned; the 700+ names matched its bucket names; the 21 April log entry matched the file timestamp

Data was primarily credit card applications; SSNs tokenized or encrypted, names/addresses/DOB/credit history not; approximately 120,000 SSNs and approximately 77,000 bank account numbers; "likely tens of millions of applications"

Capital One: about 140,000 SSNs, about 80,000 linked bank account numbers, approximately 1 million Canadian SINs, approximately 100 million US and 6 million Canadian individuals; no credit card account numbers or log-in credentials compromised
On 27 January 2021 Capital One reported approximately 4,700 additional SSNs among the accessed data

On or about 26 June 2019 "erratic" posted on a Slack channel a list of files, two of which referenced *****-WAF-Role, the directory name the Sync Command would create; the Slack channel's Meetup group listed "Paige Thompson (erratic)" as organizer

On 18 June 2019 Twitter user "ERRATIC" sent direct messages to the reporting source saying she was "dropping capitol ones dox" and "wanna distribute those buckets i think first" (the "bomb vest" message); the affiant reads this as intent to disseminate stolen data "starting with Capital One"

The Ninth Circuit names the recipient of the June 2019 Twitter messages as "cybersecurity professional Kat Valentine"; the messages "included links to the data and threats to distribute it"; Valentine reported the breach to Capital One
source: CA9 slip op. p. 7 (ca9-opinion.txt); dissent pp. 28–29 attributes the "bomb vest" message to the exchange with Valentine

claim as made in prose: Judge Sung's dissent quotes the same exchange: "Im ready to check the f*** out . . . I dont care if its jail or death. Prefer to die"; the district court found Thompson "tortured and tormented about what she did"; the majority held that finding "is not supported by the record"
source: CA9 slip op. dissent pp. 28–29; majority p. 15 (ca9-opinion.txt)

claim as made in prose: Resume on a linked GitLab page: systems engineer at the Cloud Computing Company 2015–16; Ninth Circuit: "Over two years after her employment at Amazon ended, Thompson began hacking AWS customers' accounts"

Indictment (28 Aug 2019) described "scanning software that allowed her to identify customers of a cloud computing company who had misconfigured their firewalls" and Capital One plus "more than 30 other entities"
source: DOJ indictment release 2019-08-28 (doj-indict.txt); indictment itself not fetched

claim as made in prose: Investigators have found no evidence that THOMPSON sold or disseminated any of the information she accessed
source: DOJ indictment release 2019-08-28 (doj-indict.txt); CA9 p. 6 ("did not sell or distribute any stolen information")

claim as made in prose: June 2022, seven-day trial: guilty of wire fraud, five counts of unauthorized access to a protected computer and damaging a protected computer; not guilty of access device fraud and aggravated identity theft

Ninth Circuit: "scanned millions of publicly available IP addresses associated with AWS"; "credentials from at least 200 entities and stole data from at least 30 of them"; "did not sell or distribute any stolen information"; PII of 98 million Americans
October 2022: Judge Robert S. Lasnik sentenced Thompson to time served and five years of probation; prosecutors asked for a seven-year sentence
source: DOJ sentencing release (doj-sentence.txt); CA9 pp. 8, 10 (Government argued for 84 months)

claim as made in prose: Restitution ordered at over $40 million at a separate hearing
On 17 March 2025 the Ninth Circuit vacated the sentence as substantively unreasonable; Guidelines range 168–210 months; ~98% downward variance

On 29 October 2025 the district court entered judgment on remand: time served on all counts; supervised release of 2 years on count 1 and 1 year on counts 2, 4, 5 and 8, "crediting the defendant with the 3 years of probation already served"; location monitoring (GPS) for three years "with credit for time served of three years"; 250 hours of community service; restitution of $40,745,000 to Capital One
source: Judgment in a Criminal Case, Doc. 462, sheets 1–3D and 5 (judgment-2025.txt; raw OCR judgment-2025-ocr-raw.txt)

claim as made in prose: OCC assessed an $80 million civil money penalty on 6 August 2020 (order signed 5 August 2020)
source: OCC Consent Order #2020-036 Art. III ¶1 (p. 3); OCC News Release 2020-101 (occ-news-release.txt)

claim as made in prose: The Comptroller finds, and the Bank neither admits nor denies, the following
source: OCC Consent Order #2020-036 Art. II preamble (p. 2)

claim as made in prose: OCC findings: no effective risk assessment before the ~2015 cloud migration; failures in network security controls, DLP controls and "effective dispositioning of alerts"; internal audit failed to identify weaknesses; Board failed to hold management accountable; Bank "has begun addressing the identified corrective action"
Federal Reserve cease-and-desist against Capital One Financial Corporation, 6 August 2020, "the result of a significant data breach from March 2019"; required an enhanced risk-management program
The company was fined $80 million and settled customer lawsuits for $190 million; Capital One: class settlement preliminarily approved 7 February 2022

AWS: the IMDS "runs on a special 'link local' IP address of 169.254.169.254 that means only software running on the instance can access it" and "makes the AWS credentials available for any IAM role that is attached to the instance"
The List Buckets and Sync commands were executed from Tor exit nodes and IPredator VPN addresses
Amazon statement to Krebs: "The intrusion was caused by a misconfiguration of a web application firewall and not the underlying infrastructure or the location of the infrastructure"
AWS announced IMDSv2 on 19 November 2019 in a post titled for "open firewalls, reverse proxies, and SSRF vulnerabilities"; the post does not mention Capital One

AWS: IMDSv1 "is fully secure"; IMDSv2 adds "belt and suspenders" protections for four vulnerability types; at launch "Both IMDSv1 and IMDSv2 will be available and enabled by default"; v1 kept for customers with v1 tools; CloudWatch metric for v1 calls; ec2:RoleDelivery IAM context key to restrict buckets to v2 credentials
source: AWS Security Blog 2019-11-19, paragraphs 3, 4 and final section (aws-imdsv2.txt)

claim as made in prose: IMDSv2 mechanics and rationale: PUT-initiated session token; "the vast majority do not permit HTTP PUT requests"; no tokens to callers with X-Forwarded-For; PUT plus token "always strictly more effective than requiring only a static header"; token response with IP TTL of 1 so it "will, by default, not be able to travel outside the instance"; curl recipe
